subject: political-science
lectureTitle: EU V: European Citizenship and Identity (AUW)
part: Part III · The European Union as a Political System
readings: McCormick (2021), Understanding the EU, pp. 88 to 109 · Szczerbiak and Taggart (2024), Euroscepticism and anti establishment parties in Europe, JEI 46(8)

cards.back: Rights tied to Union membership that are **additional to, not a replacement for**, national citizenship (Lisbon Art. 20).
The **gap** between the actions of the EU institutions and the ability of ordinary citizens to **directly influence** them.
Most citizens **do not understand how the EU works**, which makes public opinion unstable and easy to mislead.
Permissive consensus: citizens leave integration to the elites. Constraining dissensus: public opinion now **limits** what leaders can do (Hooghe and Marks).
Hard: opposition to EU integration **in principle** (toward leaving). Soft: opposition to the **current direction**, with membership still accepted.

cards.front: What are the **four mechanisms** that explain why a citizen supports or opposes the EU?
cards.back: **Utility** (what do I gain), **identity** (who are we), **cues** (what trusted actors say), **benchmarking** (compared with what).
As **constructed, contested and changeable**, not a fixed fact to be measured.
Civic: Europe defined by **shared values** (freedom, democracy, rule of law). Exclusionary: Europe as a **bounded cultural community** threatened by outsiders.

cards.front: What are the three types of **multi level identity**?
What is the **two way relationship** between identity and integration?
cards.back: **Identity shapes integration** (what seems legitimate) and **integration shapes identity** (through membership and socialization).
A channel letting **1 million citizens from at least 7 member states** invite the Commission to propose a law.
